newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS - Continuity promise after Danish govt shuffle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Continuity promise after Danish govt shuffle.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen was forced to reshuffle his government on Monday after the resignation of the Centre Democrat (CD) party from his Social Democrat-led coalition. He pledged political continuity.

He was speaking at a news conference after redistributing portfolios, cutting ministerial posts to 19 from 20 and boosting the strength of his Radical Liberal coalition partners to four ministers from three.
"I see it as ensuring continuity and preserving experience," he said of the reshuffled cabinet, which has one new member.
"There is much to do and there is also a steady course to maintain regarding the economy and employment," he said.

The main changes were Social Democrat Transport Minister Jan Troejborg's replacement of CD leader Mimi Jakobsen as trade and industry minister and the introduction of Radical Liberal college principal Ebbe Lundgaard as culture minister.

A second CD minister, Yvonne Herloev Andersen, was not replaced at the health ministry, which merges with the ministry of the interior. The defunct ministry's role as food watchdog passes to the former agriculture and fisheries ministry which is restructured as a "super ministry" of food.
Oversight of the financial sector -- previously shared with the finance ministry -- is to be concentrated with the economy ministry, a move welcomed by the Danish Bankers' Association.
"We have in the past seen the division between two ministries produce much inappropriate legislation," association chairman Thorleif Krarup told Reuters.
"We hope that centralisation will give the economy ministry an overview of the financial markets which is essential as the markets overlap one another more and more," he said.
The markets themselves virtually ignored the changes, trading up slightly amid the holiday torpor.
"Reaction was very limited," a bond trader said.
Jakobsen said on December 20 that her party was quitting the centre-left coalition but the five CD members of parliament would continue to vote with the minority government.
She said that her party, which had presented itself to voters as a bulwark in government against the left, was uneasy about growing dependence on the radical Socialist People's Party and Unity List.
The government made concessions to the leftists, who hold pivotal parliamentary seats, to win their support for its 1997 budget after the breakdown of its talks with the Conservatives.

Monday's reshuffle, which left the key finance, foreign affairs, economy and defence portfolios unchanged, was unlikely to alter government policies, Aalborg University political scientist Johannes Andersen told Reuters.
"Policy will not change in any way, although there could well be a change in the way things are presented," he said.
